body.heading: Patterns you can hear and feel
paragraphs: A clapping game pairs a rhyme with a repeating pattern of claps: clap your own hands, clap your partner's right hand, clap your own, clap your partner's left, clap both of theirs — and loop. The pattern is a small rhythm machine, and the rhyme is its fuel.

“Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man” is among the oldest English nursery rhymes with actions, printed in the 1700s and almost certainly older. “Miss Mary Mack”, dressed in black with silver buttons down her back, has been clapped by generations of children, the tempo rising with every verse until the pattern collapses in laughter.

body.heading: Why the pattern matters
paragraphs: The clapping pattern is a loop, and loops are how music organises time. A four-beat clapping cycle is the same skeleton as a pop song's chorus or a drum machine's bar: once you can hold a pattern steady at speed, you are doing what drummers do — subdividing time and trusting your hands.

Partners must also synchronise, which is the game's secret difficulty and its real lesson. Speed up together, recover from a fumble together, and finish together: a clapping game is teamwork rehearsed at 120 beats per minute.

body.heading: Try it: build a pattern of your own
paragraphs: Invent a four-clap pattern (self, right, self, both is a fine start), give it a two-line rhyme about someone at the table, and teach it at half speed. The rule of the playground applies: if you can teach it, you own it.

Then run the traditional experiment: repeat the pattern while gradually speeding up, and note the tempo where it breaks. That breaking point — and beating it next week — is the entire history of musical practice in miniature.

takeaway: A clapping game is a rhythm pattern with a rhyme for a motor: two players, four hands, one shared pulse.
